Being able to receive this information is known at ADS-B In.

# Airways

Airways are routes that IFR flights fly simply put.  There are 2 classes of airways, low altitude and high altitude.

Low Altitude Airways:
- For use up to, but NOT including 18,000ft MSL
- Generally class E airspace, unless crossing through other airspace 
- There are 2 types of low altitude airways:
    - Victor airways
        - Identified by a "V" followed by numbers
        - Based on VORs
        - May be flown by RNAV
        - They have a width of 4NM from centerline, unless the VORs are more than 102NM apart, then they are 4.5 degrees on either side.
        - Depicted by a black line and a black info box
    - RNAV airways or TNAV
        - Identified by a "T" followed by numbers
        - May be flown using various types of RNAV
        - Based normally on 1,200ft AGL
        - Up to but NOT including 18,000ft MSL
        - Depicted by a blue line and blue info box


High Altitude Airways:
- There are 3 types of high altitude airways:
    - Jet routes
        - Identified by a "J" followed by numbers
        - 18,000ft MSL to FL 450
        - Blue lines and info boxes are used to indicate
    - Q-routes:
        - Identified by a "Q" followed by numbers
        - 18,000ft MSL to FL 450
        - May be flown using various types of RNAV
    - Y-routes:
        - Similar to Q-routes, depicted with a "Y" followed by numbers
        - Mostly used off shore

# Class A Airspace

Class A airspace goes over all contiguous states and Alaska, from 18,000 MSL to 60,000 MSL (FL).  

ATC actively tracks and provides separation for every aircraft in class A airspace

In order to fly in class A airspace the pilot and aircraft must:
- IFR rated and current
- IFR equipped
- IFR clearance at altitude assigned by ATC
- transponder with mode C

# Class B Airspace

Class B airspace is denoted by dark blue solid lines.  You need clearance in order to enter a class B airspace.  The vertical limits are denoted by a fraction.  The numerator represents the ceiling, and the denominator represents the floor.

Typically surrounding all class B airspace, there is a Mode C veil.  This veil is a 30[[NM]] boundary around the airport that is from SFC to 10,000 MSL.  In order to enter this veil, a pilot must posses a mode C transponder and [[ADS-B Out]]

Other requirements for flying into a class B airspace is:
- Private pilot
- Student pilot with correct logbook endorsements
- Endorsement in logbook within the last 90 days competent to solo.

# Class C Airspace

Class C airspace is indicated by 2 solid magenta lines surrounding an airport.  The first circle is about 5[[NM]] in radius, and the second circle is 10[[NM]] in radius.  The floor and ceiling of each section is indicated by a bold magenta fraction.  The bottom number indicates the floor, and the top number indicates the ceiling, both in feet [[MSL]].  The 44 over SFC indicates this section starts at the surface, and ends at 4400ft [[MSL]], and the 44 over 17 means that it starts at 1700 and ends at 4400ft [[MSL]]

![[ClassCSectional.png]]

There is also a procedural outer area in a class C airspace that normally has a radius of 20[[NM]]

# Cold Front

A cold front is when a cold air mass at the surface moves, resulting in any warm airmass in it's way being pushed up and away.

A cold front typically moves at ~25-30 MPH

Typical features of a cold front are as following:
- Little warning
- Change the weather in a few hours
- Weather clears rapidly
- They're more intense

The rapid movement of warm air upwards in a cold front is conducive to creating:
- Towering cumulous clouds
- Cirriform clouds
- Cumulonimbus clouds

Depending on the intensity of the cold front, any resulting cumulonimbus clouds can also have:
- Lightning and thunder
- Hail
- Tornadoes

Sometimes a fast moving cold front can create a squall line at the font.

# Communications with Class D Airspace

While flying in a class D airspace, a VHF transmitter and receiver is required.  In order to enter, take off, or land in a class D airspace, two way communications must be established.  

If you are landing at a secondary, or satellite, airport, you must still call the primary airport.  When taking off from a secondary airport, you must call [[ATC]] as soon as practicable.

[[Class D airspace]] is in effect, as long as the tower is working and running.  If the tower is part time, then the airspace can be either [[Class E Airspace]] or [[Class G Airspace]].  Check airport listings in chart supplements for information.

# GPS

GPS is a type of RNAV that uses satellites to get the current location of an aircraft.  The GPS constellation is made up of 31 satellites that orbit the Earth at 12,000ft away from the surface.  These satellites make 2 complete orbits around earth every 24 hours.  They all are constantly transmitting signals that GPS receivers can pick up.

In order to get your location, you only need 4 satellites to be working.  One for each axis, x, y, and z, and one for any time errors

Formula for distance between satellites and receivers:
    Distance = Speed of Light X Time difference in pseudo-random code

A panel mounted GPS, which has its installation approved by the FAA, is required for IFR flight.  The GPS database must be up to date before flying IFR.  This can be checked in the flight manual supplement, to see if it is FAA approved.  The databases typically are updated every 28 days, so make sure to check.  You should be verifying the validity during both preflight and inflight.

Hand-held GPS tools can be used as an aide for situational awareness, however they can not be solely used for IFR flight.

# Hypoxia

Hypoxia is a state of oxygen deficiency in the body sufficient to impair the functions of the brain and other organs.  Hypoxia from exposure to altitude is only due to the reduced barometric pressure, as the concentration of oxygen in the atmosphere remains about 21% from the ground to space.

Symptoms of hypoxia, typically seen from 12,500ft to 15,000 include:
- Headaches
- Reduced coordination and ability to make calculations
- Worse sense of judgement
- A sense of euphoria or belligerence
- Blue coloration of fingernails and lips
- Loss of consciousness


Types of hypoxia:
- Hypoxic: Insufficient oxygen to lungs.  This can be caused by faulty equipment or misuse
- Hypemic: Blood is not able to transport sufficient oxygen to the cells in the body.  This is what carbon monoxide poisoning is.
- Histotoxic: Inability of cells to effectively use oxygen due to drugs or alcohol.


Hypoxia prevention:
- Encouraged to use supplemental oxygen above 10,000ft during the day and 5,000ft during the night
- CFRs requires flight crew to use supplemental oxygen after being between 12,500ft and 14,000ft for 30 minutes.
- All flight crew must use supplemental oxygen immediately upon going above 14,000ft
- All occupants must use supplemental oxygen above 15,000ft

# Icing

There are 3 types of Icing to be aware of when going to operate an aircraft.  There is Induction Icing, Instrument Icing, and finally Structural Icing.  

Induction Icing is defined as any icing that impedes the process of air entering the intake manifold to be mixed with fuel.  Icing on the air intakes is an obvious form of induction icing.  Another form of induction icing is carburetor icing.  This can be attributed to the incomplete vaporization of fuel in combination with the pressure decrease in the venturi.  Be aware that carb icing can occur at temperatures as warm as 70F if the air has enough moisture.  CAUTION: if carb ice occurs and you use carb heat to melt it, the engine WILL run rough for a while.  This is due to the ice melting and the water getting mixed with the fuel.

Instrument Icing is defined as icing that blocks the pitot tube or static ports of an aircraft.  The blockage of these can cause instruments to give incorrect readings, or fail completely.  The pitot-static system controls the airspeed indicator, vertical speed indicator, and the altimeter.

Lastly there is structural Icing, which is defined as, ice that forms on the surface of the aircraft.  Since airfoils generate lift by decreasing the pressure, and thus the temperature of the air around them, the propeller, the horizontal and vertical tail surfaces, and the winds, can all form ice on them at ambient temperatures that are above freezing.  

There are 3 types of structural icing:
- Rime Ice: Small amounts of moisture, such as drizzle, fog, mist, freeze upon impact with the airfoil.  Air that is trapped between the droplets is what gives the ice it's white or opaque appearance.  It typically builds up only at the leading edge, and has an irregular shape.  This makes it easy for pilots to recognize and remove it with deicing equipment.
- Clear Ice: Large super cooled water drops, found in either heavy rain or cumuliform clouds, strike the airfoil, but do not freeze immediately.  Instead, they slide back across the surface as they freeze.  Clear ice is smooth and glossy, making it very difficult to see from the cockpit.  Because it adheres to the surface beyond the leading edge, it can be difficult to remove.

Icing can not only cause there to be a loss of lift in the aircraft, due to the disruption of smooth airflow over the airfoil, but also increased drag.

# Illusions

Many different types of illusions can occur during flight.  Some can lead to spatial disorientation, while others can lead to landing errors.  Illusions rank among the most common factors cited as contributing to fatal aircraft accidents.

There are many types of illusions to be aware of:
- The leans.  An abrupt correction of a banked attitude, which has been entered into very slowly.  The inner ear doesn't sense this because the turn is so slow.  This creates an illusion of banking in the opposite direction. 
- Coriolis Illusion.  An abrupt head movement in a long held constant rate turn that has stopped stimulating the motion sensing system in the body, can create the illusion of rotation or movement on an entirely different axis.  This one is very overwhelming
- Graveyard spin.  Proper spin recovery that has ceased stimulating the motion sensing system, can create the illusion that the plane is spinning in the opposite direction.  The disoriented pilot will then put the plane into it's original spin.
- Graveyard spiral.  An observed loss of altitude in a coordinated constant rate turn that has stopped stimulating the motion sensing system, can create the illusion of being in a descent with the wings level.  The disoriented pilot will pull back on the controls, tightening the spiral and increasing the loss of altitude.

# WAAS and Non-WAAS GPS

WAAS stands for: Wide Area Augmentation System

WAAS provides higher accuracy and reliability.  WAAS GPS achieve this by using ground stations to help the satellites have better accuracy.   Also uses FDE

Non-WAAS system do not make use of the ground stations.  They instead make use of RAIM (Receiver Autonomous Integrity Monitoring)

WAAS systems are certified under TSO C145 or C146, and they are standalone, meaning you do not need any other ground avionics such as VOR, DNE, or ADF

Non-WAAS systems are certified under TSO C129 or C196, these are not standalone.  You must have avionics for ground based navigation facilities.

RNAV-1: 1NM accuracy 95% of the time
RNAV-2: 2NM accuracy 95% of the time

# Warm Front

A warm front is when a warm airmass is advancing and replacing a cold body of air.  The warm front covers the cold air from above, and then pushes it out from below.  

These fronts typically move slowly, ~10 - 15 MPH

Features of warm fronts are the following:
- Bring low ceilings
- Poor visibility and rain
- They occur more slowly
- Provide a warning
- Are generally less intense

Warm fronts tend to generate stratiform and cirrus type clouds, and fog or haze can be expected.

There is also a slight rise in barometric pressure when a warm front first moves in, that will decrease as the front passes.
